Catchability from a habitat landscape

Source: R/landscape.R
ms_landscape.Rd

Builds the catchability matrix from where stocks live and where (and how) metiers fish, instead of writing it by hand:

Usage

ms_landscape(
  cells,
  species,
  metiers,
  selectivity,
  q0 = 0.001,
  distribution = NULL
)

Arguments

cells

data frame with depth, substrate and area (any units).

species

data frame with species, depth_mean, depth_sd and one column per substrate level (weights, e.g. mud, sand, hard; missing levels get weight 0, all missing = 1).

metiers

data frame with metier, depth_min, depth_max and optional substrate (levels separated by ;, empty = all).

selectivity

gear selectivity: a matrix (metiers x species, with dimnames) or a data frame with a metier column and one column per stock. Values 0-1.

q0

catchability at average density and selectivity 1.

distribution

optional: each stock's share of its biomass in each cell (cells x stocks, columns named by stock), e.g. from species distribution models or survey hot spots. It replaces the depth and substrate preferences of species (which then only needs the column species); columns are normalised to sum to 1.

Value

A catchability matrix (metiers x stocks) with attributes distribution (cells x stocks), ground (cells x metiers, 0/1) and overlap (share of each stock on each ground).

Details

  • the seabed is a set of cells with a depth, a substrate and an area;

  • each stock's habitat suitability in a cell is a normal depth preference times a substrate weight; its distribution over the cells is suitability x area, normalised to 1;

  • each metier fishes a ground (a depth range and a set of substrates) with a gear selectivity for each stock.

The catchability of metier j for stock s is

q[j, s] = q0 x sel[j, s] x (share of s on ground j / area share of ground j)

i.e. q0 x selectivity x the stock's density on the ground relative to its average density. A stock spread evenly over the whole seabed has q = q0 x sel on every ground. The level of each stock's column is usually set afterwards by ms_condition(); the landscape gives its shape (which metiers catch the stock, and how strongly relative to each other).

See also

plot_landscape()

Examples

cells <- expand.grid(depth = seq(2.5, 77.5, 5), substrate = c("mud", "sand"))
cells$area <- 1
sp <- data.frame(species = c("A", "B"), depth_mean = c(15, 60), depth_sd = 10,
                 mud = c(1, 0.2), sand = c(0.2, 1))
mt <- data.frame(metier = c("inner", "outer"), depth_min = c(0, 40), depth_max = c(40, 80))
sel <- matrix(1, 2, 2, dimnames = list(mt$metier, sp$species))
round(ms_landscape(cells, sp, mt, sel), 5)
